title: Vision Foundation Models for Empirical Aesthetics: Representational Entropy Predicts Perceived Complexity, but Its Link to Liking Varies Across Painting Categories
content: Can the internal representations of a modern vision model capture what makes a painting look complex or appealing? We analyzed 996 paintings from the Vienna Art Picture System (VAPS) with DINOv3, a self-supervised vision foundation model. For each painting, we mapped how similar each image region was to the painting’s overall representation and quantified the irregularity of this map with permutation entropy (H), statistical complexity (C), fuzzy entropy and Lempel–Ziv complexity. Higher H, fuzzy entropy and Lempel–Ziv complexity were associated with higher perceived complexity. These associations held after accounting for low-level image properties, familiarity, painting category and art-historical period, held separately for female and male raters, and predicted complexity ratings of held-out paintings. Across all paintings, the measures showed little association with liking, and none of these associations survived adjustment for image properties. Exploratory analyses, however, revealed opposite relationships in different painting types. In paintings moving toward abstraction, a higher H value was associated with greater liking.In landscapes, higher H was associated with lower liking; however, this effect was largely attributable to differences between periods. As recognizable content becomes less prominent, aesthetic preference may depend more strongly on visual organization. On the other hand, for landscapes, the pattern is consistent with evolutionary accounts proposing that people prefer coherent, legible environments. These findings show that vision foundation models can link image representations to perceived complexity and suggest that the relationship between representational entropy and liking depends on the type of painting.
